a: comes the Christ, who is over everything, God blessed forever
t: God over all: where does the sentence stop?
p: No ancient copy settles the punctuation. It decides whether Paul calls Christ "God" or ends with praise to the Father.

readings.w: Comma after "over all": SBLGNT and the Byzantine text (Robinson-Pierpont); the words describe Christ. Read this way by Irenaeus, Tertullian and Chrysostom, and by many modern commentators
readings.orig: ὁ χριστὸς τὸ κατὰ σάρκα, ὁ ὢν ἐπὶ πάντων, θεὸς εὐλογητὸς εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας
readings.en: the Christ according to the flesh, who is over all, God blessed forever
readings.plain: comes the Christ, who is over everything, God blessed forever

readings.w: Full stop after "flesh": a doxology to God the Father. Discussed by Erasmus; printed in the text of the RSV (1946); reported as an alternative in the NA and UBS apparatus (not checked here); preferred by Käsemann
readings.orig: ὁ χριστὸς τὸ κατὰ σάρκα· ὁ ὢν ἐπὶ πάντων θεὸς εὐλογητὸς εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας
readings.en: the Christ according to the flesh. God, who is over all, be blessed forever
readings.plain: comes the Christ. God, who is over everything, be blessed forever

readings.w: Full stop after "over all": the Christ is said to be over all, and the praise goes to God (the rarer punctuation, reported by Metzger)
readings.orig: ὁ χριστὸς τὸ κατὰ σάρκα, ὁ ὢν ἐπὶ πάντων· θεὸς εὐλογητὸς εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας
readings.en: the Christ according to the flesh, who is over all. God be blessed forever
readings.plain: comes the Christ, who is over everything. God be blessed forever

why: The Plain follows the first punctuation, the one in the SBLGNT and in the majority of the church's reading since the second century. This is debated; the other two readings are real possibilities and the Greek letters are the same in all three. The oldest manuscripts have no marks that can be trusted to come from Paul, so the choice rests on grammar, style and context.
b:
For: the participle "who is" (ho on) normally describes the noun before it; "according to the flesh" invites a contrast (compare 1:3-4); in Jewish blessings the word for "blessed" (eulogetos) comes before the name of God (as in 2 Corinthians 1:3 and in the Septuagint), so a doxology to God would more naturally read "Blessed be God." Against: Paul rarely calls Christ theos (Titus 2:13 is the nearest, in a letter whose authorship is debated; John 20:28 is John, not Paul); a burst of praise to the Father suits the lament of 9:1-5. Metzger wrote a study of the question (cited below) and reports that the editors of the UBS text were divided. See the note on this phrase.

No manuscript is named here: this entry rests on the editions, the fathers as the commentaries report them, and Metzger's study. The manuscripts and any early punctuation marks in them were not checked.

p: The oldest Greek has a word for "worthless, bad"; the Byzantine text and the KJV have "evil."

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28, Tyndale House GNT, Westcott-Hort, Tregelles
readings.en: good or worthless
readings.plain: good or bad

readings.w: Byzantine text, Textus Receptus (KJV)
readings.en: good or evil
readings.plain: good or evil

why: The older reading is phaulon, a word Paul uses rarely. Copyists could easily replace it with the common kakon to match "good or evil." The same variation is reported at 2 Corinthians 5:10. The meaning is nearly the same.

a: For the Lord will carry out his word on the earth, completing it and cutting it short.
t: A longer text from the Septuagint
p: The Byzantine text and the KJV add words from Isaiah's Greek, so the verse reads more fully.

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28, Tyndale House GNT, Westcott-Hort, Tregelles (the shorter text)
readings.orig: λόγον γὰρ συντελῶν καὶ συντέμνων ποιήσει κύριος ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς
readings.en: for the Lord will do his word on the earth, completing and cutting short
readings.plain: For the Lord will carry out his word on the earth, completing it and cutting it short.

readings.w: Byzantine text, Textus Receptus (KJV)
readings.orig: λόγον γὰρ συντελῶν καὶ συντέμνων ἐν δικαιοσύνῃ· ὅτι λόγον συντετμημένον ποιήσει κύριος ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς
readings.en: for completing and cutting short in righteousness, because the Lord will do a cut-short word on the earth
readings.plain: For he is completing the word and cutting it short in righteousness, because the Lord will carry out a shortened word on the earth.

why: The shorter text is the harder one and is used by the main modern editions. The longer text is close to the Septuagint of Isaiah 10:22-23, and copyists may have filled it out from there.
b:
Isaiah 10:23 in the Hebrew is difficult, and the Greek renders it freely. The Greek verbs synteleo and syntemno can mean "complete" and "cut short," or "finish" and "decide."

Editions only; manuscript lists not checked.

a: did not arrive at that law
p: The Byzantine text repeats the words "of righteousness" and so makes the sentence smoother.

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28, Tyndale House GNT, Westcott-Hort, Tregelles (the shorter text)
readings.en: did not arrive at law
readings.plain: did not arrive at that law

readings.w: Byzantine text, Textus Receptus (KJV)
readings.en: did not arrive at the law of righteousness
readings.plain: did not arrive at the law of righteousness

why: The shorter reading is harder and explains the other: a copyist would have repeated "of righteousness" to avoid the unusual brevity.

a: as if it came by works
p: The Byzantine text and the KJV add "of the law."

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28, Tyndale House GNT, Westcott-Hort, Tregelles
readings.en: as if from works
readings.plain: as if it came by works

readings.w: Byzantine text, Textus Receptus (KJV)
readings.en: as if from works of the law
readings.plain: as if it came by works of the law

why: The shorter text is better supported, and "of the law" looks like an addition from 3:20, 28 and Galatians 2:16. The Byzantine text also adds "for" before "they stumbled," which the KJV reflects.

a: the one who believes in him
p: The Byzantine text and the KJV say "everyone who believes"; the older text has "the one who believes."

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28, Tyndale House GNT, Westcott-Hort, Tregelles
readings.en: the one believing in him
readings.plain: the one who believes in him

readings.w: Byzantine text, Textus Receptus (KJV)
readings.en: everyone believing in him
readings.plain: everyone who believes in him

why: "Everyone" is missing from the earlier text and appears in 10:11, where Paul quotes the same verse. A copyist could have brought it here from there.

p: The Byzantine text says "for Israel"; the older text has the plain pronoun "them."

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28, Tyndale House GNT
readings.en: on behalf of them
readings.plain: on their behalf

readings.w: Byzantine text, Textus Receptus (KJV)
readings.en: on behalf of Israel
readings.plain: on behalf of Israel

why: "Them" has the earlier support; "Israel" is a natural clarification, since chapter 9 ended without naming the people.

a: Moses writes that the person who does the righteousness that comes from the law will live by it.
p: Two Greek texts: one has "the righteousness" as the thing done and lived by, the other "these things" and "them."

readings.w: SBLGNT, Westcott-Hort (without "them" after "does")
readings.orig: Μωϋσῆς γὰρ γράφει ὅτι τὴν δικαιοσύνην τὴν ἐκ τοῦ νόμου ὁ ποιήσας ἄνθρωπος ζήσεται ἐν αὐτῇ
readings.en: Moses writes that the person who has done the righteousness from the law will live by it
readings.plain: Moses writes that the person who does the righteousness that comes from the law will live by it.

readings.w: NA28, NA27, Tyndale House GNT, Tregelles, Textus Receptus (KJV), Byzantine text (with "them" after "does")
readings.orig: Μωϋσῆς γὰρ γράφει τὴν δικαιοσύνην τὴν ἐκ τοῦ νόμου ὅτι ὁ ποιήσας αὐτὰ ἄνθρωπος ζήσεται ἐν αὐτοῖς
readings.en: Moses writes about the righteousness from the law that the person who has done them will live by them
readings.plain: Moses writes about the righteousness that comes from the law: that the person who does these things will live by them.

why: The editions divide, and the difference is small in meaning. The Plain departs from the NA28 and Tyndale House texts here and follows the SBLGNT. The reason is that the second reading matches the Septuagint of Leviticus 18:5 ("does them ... live by them") word for word, so a copyist could have brought it into line; the first is the harder text, since it makes "the righteousness" the thing done.

a: confess Jesus as Lord with your mouth
t: "Confess Jesus as Lord," or "confess the word, that Jesus is Lord"?
p: One text has an object ("Jesus as Lord"); another has "the word ... that Jesus is Lord," echoing 10:8.

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28, NA27, Tyndale House GNT, Tregelles, Textus Receptus, Byzantine text (the KJV renders it "the Lord Jesus")
readings.orig: ἐὰν ὁμολογήσῃς ἐν τῷ στόματί σου κύριον Ἰησοῦν
readings.en: if you confess in your mouth Jesus as Lord
readings.plain: confess Jesus as Lord with your mouth

readings.w: Westcott-Hort; also the base text behind this site's word-by-word line (the TAGNT), which has "the word" and the nominative "Lord Jesus"
readings.orig: ἐὰν ὁμολογήσῃς τὸ ῥῆμα ἐν τῷ στόματί σου ὅτι κύριος Ἰησοῦς
readings.en: if you confess the word in your mouth, that Jesus is Lord
readings.plain: confess the word with your mouth, that Jesus is Lord

why: The accusative "Jesus as Lord" is in the editions of nearly every kind, including the Byzantine text. The longer reading echoes the "word" of 10:8 and Deuteronomy 30:14, and copyists may have added it for that reason, or dropped it. The meaning is the same: the content of the confession is "Jesus is Lord."

a: those who tell the good news of good things
p: The Byzantine text and the KJV add "of peace" and repeat the verb, echoing the words of Isaiah's Greek.

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28, NA27, Tyndale House GNT (Westcott-Hort and Tregelles also lack the article before "good things")
readings.en: of those bringing good news of good things
readings.plain: those who tell the good news of good things

readings.w: Byzantine text, Textus Receptus (KJV)
readings.orig: τῶν εὐαγγελιζομένων εἰρήνην, τῶν εὐαγγελιζομένων τὰ ἀγαθά
readings.en: of those bringing good news of peace, of those bringing good news of good things
readings.plain: those who tell the good news of peace, who tell the good news of good things

why: The shorter text has the stronger support. The longer text echoes the "peace" and the "good things" of Isaiah 52:7, and copyists may have supplied them from there. The Septuagint of Isaiah, like the Hebrew, speaks of one herald; the plural "those who tell" is Paul's own.

p: The older Greek says "Christ"; the Byzantine text and the KJV say "God."

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28, NA27, Tyndale House GNT, Westcott-Hort, Tregelles
readings.en: through a word of Christ
readings.plain: the word of Christ

readings.w: Byzantine text, Textus Receptus (KJV)
readings.en: through a word of God
readings.plain: the word of God

why: "Christ" is the harder reading, since the phrase "word of Christ" is unusual in Paul (compare Colossians 3:16), and "word of God" is the common phrase a copyist would reach for.

a: If it did, grace would no longer be grace.
t: A second half of the verse in the Byzantine text
p: Many manuscripts and the KJV add a sentence that says the same thing from the other side.

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28, NA27, Tyndale House GNT, Westcott-Hort, Tregelles
readings.orig: εἰ δὲ χάριτι, οὐκέτι ἐξ ἔργων, ἐπεὶ ἡ χάρις οὐκέτι γίνεται χάρις
readings.en: if by grace, no longer from works, since grace would no longer be grace
readings.plain: If it did, grace would no longer be grace.

readings.w: Byzantine text, Textus Receptus (KJV)
readings.orig: ... ἐπεὶ ἡ χάρις οὐκέτι γίνεται χάρις. εἰ δὲ ἐξ ἔργων, οὐκέτι ἐστὶν χάρις· ἐπεὶ τὸ ἔργον οὐκέτι ἐστὶν ἔργον
readings.en: ... since grace would no longer be grace. But if from works, it is no longer grace; since work would no longer be work
readings.plain: If it did, grace would no longer be grace. But if it comes from works, it is no longer grace; otherwise work would no longer be work.

why: The shorter text is the older and the harder. The extra sentence looks like a balancing second half added by copyists who wanted the argument to be stated from both sides.

a: Now I am speaking to you Gentiles
p: The Byzantine text and the KJV connect the verse to the one before with "for" instead of "but, now."

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28, Tyndale House GNT, Westcott-Hort, Tregelles
readings.en: but to you I speak, the Gentiles
readings.plain: Now I am speaking to you Gentiles

readings.w: Byzantine text, Textus Receptus (KJV)
readings.en: for to you I speak, the Gentiles
readings.plain: For I am speaking to you Gentiles

why: "Now" marks the turn to a new address and has the earlier support; "for" is a smoother connection that copyists could have preferred.
b:
The two texts also differ over a small word after "apostle" in 11:13: the SBLGNT and others read "indeed therefore" (men oun), the Byzantine text only "indeed" (men). The Plain does not show it.

Editions only; manuscript lists not checked.

a: a sharer in the rich root of the olive tree
t: "The rich root," or "the root and the richness"?
p: Some Greek texts have an extra "and", which splits one rich root into two things.

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28, NA27, Tyndale House GNT, Westcott-Hort (no "and")
readings.orig: συγκοινωνὸς τῆς ῥίζης τῆς πιότητος τῆς ἐλαίας
readings.en: a fellow-sharer of the root of the richness of the olive tree
readings.plain: a sharer in the rich root of the olive tree

readings.w: Tregelles, Textus Receptus (the KJV has "the root and fatness"), Byzantine text (with "and")
readings.orig: συγκοινωνὸς τῆς ῥίζης καὶ τῆς πιότητος τῆς ἐλαίας
readings.en: a fellow-sharer of the root and of the richness of the olive tree
readings.plain: a sharer in the root and the richness of the olive tree

why: The Plain follows the SBLGNT, which agrees here with the NA28 and the Tyndale House text. "Root of the richness" is an odd phrase, and the extra "and" smooths it into two plain nouns, so a copyist may have added it. The meaning is close either way: the wild branch shares in the nourishing root.

a: he will not spare you either
p: The Byzantine text and the KJV add a word that makes the verse a warning ("take heed lest").

readings.w: SBLGNT, Tyndale House GNT, Westcott-Hort, Tregelles (without the word)
readings.en: neither will he spare you
readings.plain: he will not spare you either

readings.w: NA28 (the word in square brackets) and NA27, Textus Receptus (KJV), Byzantine text
readings.en: lest perhaps he will not spare you either
readings.plain: he may not spare you either

why: The SBLGNT omits the word; the NA28 prints it in square brackets, showing its editors were unsure. Without it the verse is a flat statement; with it the verse is a caution. The sense is close either way, since 11:22 gives the same warning.

a: they also may now be shown mercy
p: Some editions have "now" twice in the verse; others only once.

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28 (the word in square brackets), NA27, Westcott-Hort
readings.en: so that they also now may be shown mercy
readings.plain: they also may now be shown mercy

readings.w: Tyndale House GNT, Tregelles, Textus Receptus (KJV), Byzantine text
readings.en: so that they also may be shown mercy
readings.plain: they also may be shown mercy

why: The editions divide. The second "now" puts Israel's mercy in the same present as the Gentiles' mercy, which suits the argument (see the note on 11:31). It may also have been added to match the first "now." It matters because it bears on whether Israel's turning is future only or already begun.
